title: Causes of Dyslexia (Etiology)
description: Dyslexia has a multifactorial etiology involving complex interactions between genetic predisposition, neurobiological differences, cognitive processing deficits, and environmental influences.

sections.name: Genetic Factors
sections.description: Dyslexia has substantial genetic contributions, with heritability estimates ranging from 40% to 80% based on twin and family studies.
keyPoints: A 2022 genome-wide association study (GWAS) of 51,800 adults with dyslexia identified 42 independent genome-wide significant loci
15 of these loci are in genes linked to cognitive ability/educational attainment
27 are new and potentially more specific to dyslexia
Commonly replicated candidate genes include DCDC2, KIAA0319, and DYX1C1
Genetic correlation between males and females is 0.91, indicating similar genetic etiology
Polygenic risk scores can explain a portion of variance in reading ability, though prediction accuracy remains limited for clinical use

specificGenes.name: DCDC2
specificGenes.function: Associated with neural migration patterns and white matter connectivity
specificGenes.finding: READ1 deletion in DCDC2 gene is associated with lower global efficiency, local efficiency, and clustering coefficient in white matter networks

specificGenes.name: KIAA0319
specificGenes.function: Regulates cell cycle during human neuroepithelial cell development

geneEnvironmentInteractions: Low socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with higher probability of dyslexia and exacerbates genetic contribution
Parental education moderates the effect of genetic risk variants on reading ability
Environmental pollutants may selectively target dyslexia-related genes

sections.name: Neurological Factors
sections.description: Dyslexia is associated with differences in brain structure and function, particularly in regions involved in reading and language processing.
keyPoints: Brain differences are observed in both gray matter and white matter
Functional MRI studies show altered activation patterns during reading tasks
Machine learning approaches using neuroimaging data show classification accuracy of 65-90% in controlled cohorts
These findings have limited generalizability to real-world populations and should not be confused with clinical diagnostic utility

grayMatter: Differences in gray matter volume in left occipito-temporal cortex (including visual word form area)
Note: Replication of these findings has been inconsistent
whiteMatter: Reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) reported in arcuate fasciculus in some studies
Connectivity differences in left perisylvian language network
READ1 deletion in DCDC2 gene associated with lower network efficiency

functionalDifferences: Hypoactivation in left hemisphere reading networks (occipito-temporal, temporoparietal, inferior frontal regions)
Compensatory hyperactivation in right hemisphere homologues in some individuals
Altered functional connectivity during reading tasks
Deficits in neural entrainment and temporal processing, particularly in auditory and speech processing networks

sections.name: Cognitive Factors
sections.description: Cognitive processing deficits play a key role in dyslexia, with phonological processing being the most consistently identified deficit.
keyPoints: The phonological deficit hypothesis remains the most supported cognitive account of dyslexia
Double-deficit hypothesis proposes combinations of phonological and rapid automatized naming (RAN) deficits
Working memory, processing speed, and attention show mixed evidence for involvement

phonologicalDeficit.description: The most consistently supported cognitive account of dyslexia
evidence: Phonological awareness deficits in dyslexia across languages and orthographies
Phonological processing impairments predict reading difficulties
Phonological deficits are evident in both children and adults with dyslexia

doubleDeficit.description: Dyslexia can arise from combinations of deficits
doubleDeficit.evidence: Evidence supports distinct subtypes with single and double deficits

rapidAutomatedNaming.description: RAN deficits are consistently observed in dyslexia
evidence: RAN speed correlates with reading fluency
RAN deficits persist even when phonological awareness is intact
RAN and phonological awareness contribute independently to reading ability

otherCognitiveFactors.evidence: Mixed evidence - some studies show verbal working memory impairments, others find deficits only when phonological processing demands are high
Slower naming speed (RAN) is a robust finding, but general processing speed deficits are less consistent
Mixed - some studies report attention control difficulties, others find attention deficits only in comorbid ADHD. Not considered a core feature of dyslexia

sections.name: Environmental Factors
sections.description: Environmental factors influence dyslexia risk and outcomes, often interacting with genetic predisposition.
keyPoints: Socioeconomic status consistently affects dyslexia risk and outcomes
Prenatal and perinatal factors may contribute to risk
Educational quality and instruction affect dyslexia outcomes
Gene-environment interactions play a significant role
socioeconomicStatus: Low SES is associated with higher prevalence of reading difficulties
SES moderates genetic risk - low SES exacerbates genetic contribution
SES affects access to early intervention and educational resources
prenatalPerinatal: Some studies link prenatal exposure to environmental pollutants to dyslexia risk
Preterm birth and low birth weight associated with increased risk
Prenatal nutrition may play a role (evidence emerging)
educationalFactors: Quality of reading instruction moderates expression of dyslexia
Early identification and intervention improve outcomes
Educational policies affect identification rates and support access

multipleDeficitModel.description: The multiple-deficit model proposes that dyslexia arises from combinations of cognitive risk factors rather than a single core deficit

comorbidityPatterns.description: Dyslexia frequently co-occurs with other neurodevelopmental disorders
comorbidityPatterns.note: Comorbidity suggests shared genetic and neurobiological risk factors

disclaimer: Etiological factors show both consistency and variation across individuals. Genetic factors are largely language-independent, while neurological and cognitive factors are moderated by orthographic depth and language characteristics.
